samples.text:
In some cities, drivers have to pay money if they want to drive into the city centre during the busy times of the day. I think this policy has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that it reduce traffic. When people have to pay every day, many of them will decide to use the bus, the train or a bicycle instead of their car. As a result, the roads in the centre are less crowded and the journeys become faster for buses, taxis and delivery vans. The second advantage is about the environment. Less cars means less air pollution and less noise, so the city centre become a healthier and more pleasant place for people who live and work there. In addition, the government can use the money from the charge to improve public transport, for example by buying new buses.

However, this system also has some disadvantages. It is unfair for people with low income, because rich people can pay the fee easily but poor people cannot. Also, some people have no choice and they must use their car, for example workers who start very early in the morning when there is no buses. Shop owners in the centre are also worried that fewer customers will come to their shops.

In conclusion, charging drivers to enter the city centre can cause some problems, especially for poor people and small shops. However, I believe the benefits for traffic and the environment are more important, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. The government should use the money to make public transport cheaper and better for everyone.
samples.why: Clear position and judgement · relevant main ideas but support is brief and general · mechanical linking (The first, The second, Also) · adequate vocabulary · agreement and countability errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
Several major cities have introduced congestion charges, which require motorists to pay a fee for driving into the centre during peak hours. Although this measure can place a burden on some groups, I am convinced that its benefits outweigh its drawbacks.

The principal advantage is a reduction in traffic. Faced with a daily charge, many commuters switch to public transport, cycling or car-sharing, and the remaining traffic can move more freely. This benefits not only drivers but also buses and emergency vehicles, which are otherwise delayed by congestion. A second benefit is environmental. Fewer vehicles in central areas leads to cleaner air and less noise, improving the health and quality of life of residents and people who work there. In addition, the money raised can be invested directly in public transport, creating a positive cycle in which better services encourage even more people to leave their cars at home.

On the other hand, critics raise some valid points. The fee affects low-income drivers far more than wealthy ones, who may simply regard it as a minor expense. People who have little choice but to drive, such as those working night shifts or living in areas with poor transport links, may feel they are being punished. Some businesses in the centre also worry that the charge will discourage shoppers and push them towards out-of-town shopping centres.

However, these concerns can be addressed through careful design of the scheme. Discounts for residents, exemptions for disabled drivers and improvements to bus services before the charge is introduced can make the system considerably fairer.

In conclusion, although congestion charges may be unfair to certain groups and could affect some businesses, they are an effective way to cut traffic and pollution. On balance, therefore, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported, with counter-arguments addressed · clear topic in each paragraph · good range of vocabulary (peak hours, transport links) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Charging motorists to enter city centres at peak times has been adopted by a number of cities seeking to tackle congestion and pollution. Although the policy raises legitimate questions of fairness, I believe that, when well designed, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

The rationale for such charges is that road space in a city centre is a scarce resource which, when provided free, is inevitably overused. By attaching a price to driving at the busiest times, a congestion charge encourages motorists to reconsider journeys that are not essential, to travel at quieter times or to switch to public transport. The result is faster, more reliable journeys for buses, deliveries and emergency services, whose efficiency is vital to the functioning of a city. The environmental gains are equally significant: reduced traffic means lower emissions and less noise in precisely the places where people are most concentrated. Moreover, the revenue generated can be ring-fenced for improving public transport, so that the alternatives to driving become steadily more attractive.

The main objection is that a flat fee is regressive. For a well-paid professional, the charge may be a trivial inconvenience, whereas for a low-paid worker who depends on a car, it can represent a substantial share of their daily earnings. Retailers in central districts also fear a loss of trade if shoppers choose to drive to suburban malls instead.

These concerns deserve serious attention, but they are arguments for refining the scheme rather than rejecting it. Exemptions for residents and disabled drivers, discounts for essential workers and investment in affordable public transport can all reduce the unequal impact, while a less congested, more pleasant centre may in fact attract more visitors on foot.

In conclusion, although congestion charges can bear more heavily on those with lower incomes, their capacity to reduce traffic, cut pollution and fund better transport makes them, on balance, a worthwhile policy whose benefits outweigh its costs.
samples.why: Fully developed response with a clear, reasoned judgement · counter-arguments evaluated rather than listed · skilful paragraphing and cohesion · precise, sophisticated vocabulary (regressive, ring-fenced) · wide range of accurate structures.
